title: Hassan ibn Thabit
hook: the poet of the Prophet ﷺ, who defended him in verse

segments.voice: Yesterday: Umm Sulaym, who asked for faith as her dowry and gave hard news as a loan returned. Your line was faith for a dowry.

Lines of verse mocking the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, are passing from mouth to mouth. Not arrows. Rhymes. A sharp line is easy to remember, and it can make a man look like a fool to people who have never met him. So what does a community do when it's attacked in verse? Ignore it? Answer with force? Or find a poet of its own. Today: Hassan ibn Thabit, who answered.
screen: `VERSES MOCKING THE PROPHET.` → `NOT ARROWS. RHYMES.` → `WHO WOULD ANSWER?`

segments.voice: Hassan was a man of Medina and a poet. Sahih al-Bukhari keeps the Prophet's charge to him. In one report, the Prophet tells Hassan to answer the poets who were mocking, and says that Gabriel is with him. In another: answer on my behalf, and he prays, O God, support him with the Holy Spirit. A poet, told his verses had help from heaven. Then the pulpit. Aisha reports, in the collections of Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi, that the Prophet had a pulpit set up for Hassan in the mosque, where Hassan would stand and defend the Prophet in verse. Poetry, in the place of prayer, on a raised step, with permission. Not everyone was comfortable with that. Bukhari tells a scene after the Prophet's death. Umar passes Hassan reciting in the mosque and shows his disapproval. Hassan doesn't back down. I used to recite in here, he says, when someone better than you was present. Then he turns to Abu Hurayrah and asks, by God, whether he heard the Prophet say: answer on my behalf, O God, support him with the Holy Spirit. Abu Hurayrah says yes. Hassan took the weapon being used against the community and turned it into a defense, with the Prophet's blessing, in the open. Words can wound. His answer was more words, placed where everyone could hear.
screen: `ANSWER ON MY BEHALF.` · `SUPPORT HIM WITH THE HOLY SPIRIT.` · `A PULPIT IN THE MOSQUE.` · `UMAR FROWNS; HASSAN STANDS FIRM.` · then, large: `THE POET'S PULPIT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone or something that deserves honoring: a friend talked about unfairly, a teacher, a place you love, or, if you pray, God. Find four short lines in praise, slowly, one for each breath; they don't need to rhyme, and true lines are better than clever ones.
Hassan, the poet of Medina given a pulpit in the mosque to answer the Prophet's critics in verse, with the Prophet's own blessing. Today's word.
Your line: the poet's pulpit. Verse, answered with more verse, in the open. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Muslims remember Hassan ibn Thabit as the poet of the Prophet, from reports in Bukhari and in Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi that a pulpit was set up for him in the mosque, and some Muslims still recite poems in praise of the Prophet today.

original.note: Arabic: Hassan, son of Thabit, the poet of the Prophet.

trapdoor: what you thought: a poet who wrote nice verses about the Prophet.
what it means: in a world where poems traveled like news, he answered attacks in verse, from a pulpit in the mosque.
what a scholar hears: Bukhari has 'answer on my behalf' and 'support him with the Holy Spirit'; Aisha's report of the pulpit is in Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi.

chat.says: How did the Prophet respond when people mocked him in poems?
options: He asked Hassan to answer in verse, and a pulpit was set up for him.
He banned all poetry in Medina so the mocking couldn't spread.
He ignored it, and told his companions never to reply at all.
chat.meaning: Bukhari: answer on my behalf; O God, support him with the Holy Spirit. Aisha reports a pulpit set up for Hassan in the mosque.

Hassan ibn Thabit.meaning: a poet of Medina who defended the Prophet in verse

Gabriel.meaning: the angel of revelation; Jibril in Arabic

Aisha.meaning: a wife of the Prophet, who reported the pulpit

al-Tirmidhi.meaning: compiler of a major hadith collection

Abu Hurayrah.meaning: a companion who confirmed the Prophet's words
